kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-02.title: Semicircles minus overlaps
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-02.body:
Each side carries two semicircles of diameter 2 (radius 1). In the picture a region is grey when it is covered by exactly one semicircle; where two semicircles overlap (the lens at each corner) it is white again.

- Total area of the semicircles: $8 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = 4\pi$.
- At a corner, the two semicircles centred at distance 1 from the corner overlap in a lens made of two quarter-circle segments: $2\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac12\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1$. Four corners: $2\pi - 4$.

Grey area $=$ (sum of semicircles) $- 2 \times$ (overlaps) $= 4\pi - 2(2\pi - 4) = 8$.

White area $= 16 - 8 = 8$.

**Answer: (B) 8**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-02.title: White = centre + lenses
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-02.body:
The white part consists of the central region (outside all semicircles) and the four white lenses at the corners.

- The union of the semicircles has area (sum) $-$ (overlaps) $= 4\pi - (2\pi - 4) = 2\pi + 4$, using the lens area $\frac{\pi}{2} - 1$ from the first solution. So the central region has area $16 - (2\pi + 4) = 12 - 2\pi$.
- The four lenses have area $2\pi - 4$.

White area: $(12 - 2\pi) + (2\pi - 4) = 8$ — the $\pi$'s cancel.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-09.title: Scale the lengths
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-09.body:
1 cm on the plan is 50 cm in reality. So the apartment measures $20 \cdot 50 = 1000$ cm $= 10$ m by $30 \cdot 50 = 1500$ cm $= 15$ m. Its area is $10 \cdot 15 = 150$ m².

**Answer: (B) 150 m²**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-09.title: Scale the area
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-09.body:
Areas scale with the square of the scale: the plan area $600$ cm² becomes $600 \cdot 50^2 = 1\,500\,000$ cm² $= 150$ m² (since $1$ m² $= 10\,000$ cm²).

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-17.title: Common base PQ
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-17.body:
Both triangles have the base $PQ$ on line $b$. The big triangle has its third vertex on $a$, so its height is the distance $h_1$ between $a$ and $b$; the small one has its third vertex on $c$, height $h_2$ = distance between $b$ and $c$.

$$\tfrac12 PQ\cdot h_1 = 10, \qquad \tfrac12 PQ \cdot h_2 = 5.$$
Adding: $\frac12 PQ (h_1 + h_2) = 15$, and $h_1 + h_2 = 6$, so $3\, PQ = 15$ and $PQ = 5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-17.title: Ratio of heights
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-17.body:
Same base, so the areas are in the ratio of the heights: $h_1 : h_2 = 10 : 5 = 2 : 1$. With $h_1 + h_2 = 6$: $h_1 = 4$, $h_2 = 2$. Then $\frac12 \cdot PQ \cdot 4 = 10$ gives $PQ = 5$.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-20.title: List them
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-20.body:
Let the sides be $a < b < c$ (scalene) with $a + b > c$ and $a + b + c \le 10$.

- $a = 1$: we would need $c < 1 + b$, i.e. $c \le b$ — impossible since $c > b$.
- $a = 2$: $c < b + 2$ and $c > b$ force $c = b + 1$; perimeter $2b + 3 \le 10$ gives $b \le 3$, so $b = 3$, $c = 4$: triangle $(2, 3, 4)$.
- $a = 3$: $b \ge 4$, $c \ge 5$, perimeter $\ge 12$ — too big.

Only $(2, 3, 4)$.

**Answer: (B) 1**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-20.title: Check the perimeters
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-20.body:
The smallest scalene integer triangles are $(2,3,4)$ with perimeter 9, then $(2,4,5)$ and $(3,4,5)$ with perimeters 11 and 12. Triples like $(1,2,3)$, $(2,3,5)$, $(1,3,4)$ are degenerate or impossible. So there is exactly one with perimeter below 11.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-23.title: The angles at O fill a full turn
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-23.body:
As in the diagram, the triangles go all the way round $O$, so with $n$ triangles
$$m + 2m + \dots + nm = m\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = 360.$$
So $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ must be a divisor of 360, and $m = 360 \div \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

- $m = 1$ needs $n(n+1) = 720$: but $26\cdot 27 = 702$, $27 \cdot 28 = 756$ — impossible.
- $m = 2$ needs $n(n+1) = 360$: $18 \cdot 19 = 342$, $19 \cdot 20 = 380$ — impossible.
- $m = 3$ needs $n(n+1) = 240 = 15 \cdot 16$ ✓, so $n = 15$.

For $m = 3$ take 15 isosceles triangles with apex $O$, all with legs of the same length and apex angles $3^\circ, 6^\circ, \dots, 45^\circ$ (sum $3 \cdot 120 = 360^\circ$). Neighbours share a full leg, so this arrangement works.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-25.title: Factor the vertex sum
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-25.body:
Let the pairs of opposite faces carry $a, a'$; $b, b'$; $c, c'$. Every vertex touches exactly one face from each pair, and each choice of one face from each pair gives exactly one vertex. So the sum of the 8 vertex products is
$$(a + a')(b + b')(c + c') = 1001 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13.$$
Each bracket is at least 2, so the three brackets must be 7, 11 and 13 in some order (1001 has no other factorisation into three factors $\ge 2$). The sum of the face numbers is $7 + 11 + 13 = 31$.

**Answer: (E) 31**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-29.title: Find the rectangle
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-29.body:
The long cut goes from the top-left corner down to the bottom side; it has length $5 + 10 = 15$ and drops by the height 9. By Pythagoras its horizontal extent is $\sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = 12$.

The short vertical cut stands on this line one third of the way along it ($5$ of $15$), so it is $\frac13 \cdot 12 = 4$ from the left side. The top side is therefore $4 + 12 = 16$ long.

The rectangle is $16 \times 9$ with area $144$. The square made from the same pieces has the same area, so its side is $12$ and its perimeter $48$.

**Answer: (B) 48**

kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-30.title: Relative motion
kangaroo-ca-2013-g0910-30.body:
Let the pipe have length $L$ and let the pipe move $r$ metres while Yurko takes one pace (1 m).

- Walking with the tractor: in 140 paces Yurko walks 140 m and the pipe moves $140r$, so $L = 140 - 140r$.
- Walking against it: $L = 20 + 20r$.

So $140 - 140r = 20 + 20r$, giving $r = \frac34$ and $L = 20 + 15 = 35$ m.

**Answer: (B) 35 m**
